title: Example: bounds, ROB and your own loop
description: Base and V1 on processor B4: predict, check a bound, size the ROB and write a faster version of the loop.

tutorial.name: Lesson L1: bounds, ROB and your own loop

steps.title: Lesson L1
steps.description:
This lesson has 4 tasks: a prediction, a question and two goals.
The bar above shows your progress; when every task is done it shows your completion code.
You can use the programs {{program}}, V1 and V2 on processor {{processor}}, with N = {{N}}.

steps.title: Task 1: predict
steps.description:
Before simulating, predict the cycles per iteration of {{program}} on {{processor}}.
Hint: two additions of {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}} cycles depend on each other in every iteration.
Write your prediction, Save it, and then run the simulation.

steps.title: Task 2: the latency bound
steps.questionText: Open Static Analysis: what is the latency bound of {{program}} on {{processor}} (cycles/iter)?
steps.numericCorrect: Right: the chain of sum has two additions of {{latency.FLOAT.ADD}} cycles, {{latencyBound}} cycles/iter.
steps.numericWrong: Look at the row tagged max of the Latency bounds table.

steps.title: Program V1
steps.description:
V1 adds V[i] + W[i] first, and only then adds the result to sum:
the chain of sum has a single addition per iteration, so V1 can run twice as fast as Base.
But to overlap iterations, the processor needs room for many instructions in flight: the ROB.

steps.title: Task 3: size the ROB
steps.description:
With ROB 64, V1 runs about 2 cycles/iter. Find the smallest ROB that keeps it below 2.1 cycles/iter.
Click the ROB cell of the processor to change it (now allowed), and simulate after each change.
The goal is achieved once; keep trying to lower the ROB: your best value is recorded.

steps.title: Task 4: your own loop
steps.description:
Write your own version of the loop with Edit Program (top bar), save it with a new name
(it is added to the list) and simulate it. Goal: less than 3 cycles per algorithmic operation
(cycles/iter ÷ S, where S is the number of elements added per iteration).
It must be your program: Base, V1 and V2 do not count.

steps.title: End of the lesson
steps.description:
When the 4 tasks are done, the bar shows your completion code: give it to your teacher with your NIU.
Exit lesson returns the simulator to its state before the lesson.
